authored_claims.normalizedClaim: In a small randomized, open-label study of 56 people with ulcerative colitis in remission who had iron-deficiency anaemia, the researchers did not detect a statistically significant difference in haemoglobin, red-cell indices or iron measures between daily and alternate-day oral iron after 8 weeks, and adverse events and flares were also not significantly different between the groups. This does not prove that the two schedules are equivalent, and it is not a recommendation to change iron dosing: talk to a clinician before changing how you take iron.
authored_claims.exactSupportingExcerpt: Our study did not show any significant difference in mean hemoglobin levels, RBC indices, or iron profiles between the daily and alternate-day oral iron groups. Adverse events and disease flare were also not statistically significant in the two groups.
authored_claims.studyPopulation: Adults with ulcerative colitis in remission and iron-deficiency anaemia (n = 56)
authored_claims.studyDesign: Randomized, open-label trial; daily vs alternate-day oral iron; primary outcome mean change in haemoglobin at 8 weeks
authored_claims.limitations: 56 participants, open-label, 8 weeks, one oral iron formulation, single country; the authors say larger studies are needed. 'No significant difference' does not prove the two schedules are equivalent.

authored_claims.normalizedClaim: A German guideline update on ulcerative colitis surgery (status November 2025) states that in acute severe ulcerative colitis, colectomy (surgery to remove the colon) is still indicated when standard drug treatment has failed; in selected cases a JAK inhibitor can be considered as an alternative third-line treatment in specialised centres.
authored_claims.exactSupportingExcerpt: In patients with acute severe ulcerative colitis, colectomy is still indicated for treatment after failure of standard pharmacotherapy, in selected cases a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor can be considered as an alternative third line treatment in centers.
authored_claims.exactLocator: PubMed abstract (PMID 43026331), first sentence; Chirurgie 2026 (German-language guideline summary with English abstract)
authored_claims.studyPopulation: Adults with acute severe ulcerative colitis who failed standard pharmacotherapy
authored_claims.studyDesign: National clinical practice guideline (surgery chapter), abstract-level summary
authored_claims.evidenceStrength: national guideline statement (abstract only; strength-of-recommendation grading not stated in the abstract)
authored_claims.limitations: German national guideline summarised in a journal abstract; the recommendation grade, evidence level and the full text were not read. Applicability to Canada/US care pathways is not assessed. Decisions about surgery are made with the treating team.

authored_claims.normalizedClaim: STRIDE-III (2026, updating STRIDE-II) lists histological remission in ulcerative colitis as an 'adjunctive' treatment target: studies link it with favourable outcomes and it can guide treatment optimisation and closer monitoring, but it does not necessarily require a change in the type of medicine. This is an expert consensus statement, not a recommendation for any one person.
authored_claims.exactSupportingExcerpt: Adjunctive targets (ie, urgency, histological remission in ulcerative colitis, transmural remission in Crohn's disease, and growth) are supported by studies showing association with favourable outcomes and guide treatment optimisation and tighter monitoring but do not necessarily require a change in therapeutic class.
authored_claims.exactLocator: PubMed abstract (PMID 42896564), Findings; Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2026
authored_claims.studyPopulation: People with inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, adult and paediatric); statement names UC explicitly
authored_claims.studyDesign: Systematic review (13,071 records, 1,018 included) + surveys + modified Delphi consensus (IOIBD / Porto group)
authored_claims.evidenceStrength: expert consensus (systematic review + Delphi; >=75% agreement threshold)
authored_claims.limitations: Abstract-level only (full text and the voting results for this statement were not read). The source covers IBD generally; this statement names UC explicitly. Targets guide clinicians and are not a treatment plan for an individual.

CLM-115.patient: AGA suggests that for people with ulcerative colitis who are in symptomatic remission (feeling well), a biomarker test, such as a stool test, may help monitoring when it is used together with symptoms rather than relying on symptoms alone. Your clinician decides which tests are right for you.
CLM-115.reason: UC-specific AGA practice guideline recommendation; excerpt is verbatim and the claim restates it without adding.
CLM-115.limitations_extra: Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.

CLM-116.patient: For people with ulcerative colitis in symptomatic remission, AGA suggests that a fecal calprotectin below 150 µg/g, a normal fecal lactoferrin and/or a normal CRP may help rule out active inflammation, so that routine endoscopy may not be needed. 150 µg/g is a guideline decision threshold, not a diagnosis for any one person: results vary between tests and between days. Your clinician interprets them with your symptoms and decides whether an endoscopy is needed; do not skip or delay a scope or a clinic visit because of a test result.
CLM-116.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation; thresholds are decision thresholds, not individual diagnoses (stated in limitations).
CLM-116.limitations_extra: Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.

CLM-117.patient: For people with ulcerative colitis who have moderate-to-severe symptoms, AGA suggests that a fecal calprotectin above 150 µg/g, an elevated fecal lactoferrin or an elevated CRP may help a clinician decide on treatment without routine endoscopy. 150 µg/g is a guideline threshold, not a diagnosis for any one person, and any treatment change is decided by your clinician, not by a test result alone.
CLM-117.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation; verbatim excerpt.
CLM-117.limitations_extra: Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.

CLM-118.patient: When symptoms and biomarker tests disagree (for example feeling well but with raised markers, or moderate-to-severe symptoms with normal markers), AGA suggests that a clinician may consider an endoscopic assessment before adjusting treatment. Do not change your treatment yourself.
CLM-118.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation addressing a common patient question (do symptoms always match inflammation?).
CLM-118.limitations_extra: Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.

CLM-119.patient: For people with ulcerative colitis who have only mild symptoms, AGA suggests that an endoscopic assessment of disease activity may be used to help a clinician make treatment decisions.
CLM-119.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline recommendation; verbatim excerpt.
CLM-119.limitations_extra: Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.

CLM-120.patient: The AGA guideline panel identified the choice between biomarker-based monitoring and endoscopy-based monitoring as a knowledge gap, so it is not known which approach is better. This means the guideline's biomarker suggestions should not be read as showing that biomarkers are better than endoscopy.
CLM-120.reason: UC-specific AGA statement of uncertainty. Owner asked for 'no recommendation for or against ... for improving long-term outcomes'; the public abstract only says 'knowledge gap', so the wording stays within the abstract and the phrase about long-term outcomes needs the full text.
CLM-120.limitations_extra: Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.

CLM-121.patient: The AGA guideline concludes that non-invasive tests - fecal calprotectin, fecal lactoferrin and blood CRP - can inform monitoring and management of ulcerative colitis. Your clinician decides how to use them for you.
CLM-121.reason: UC-specific AGA guideline conclusion; verbatim excerpt.
CLM-121.limitations_extra: Wording edited after owner safety review (2026-11-17); 'suggests'/'may' mirror the conditional GRADE recommendation. Not a basis for changing treatment or skipping endoscopy.

CLM-126.patient: The STRIDE-II consensus says histological healing in ulcerative colitis is not a formal treatment target but should be assessed as a measure of how deep remission is.
CLM-126.reason: IBD-general consensus with an explicit ulcerative-colitis statement; the claim keeps the source's 'not a formal target' wording. If approved its claim-level applicability is recorded as ulcerative_colitis (the source stays IBD-general) so the app can serve it.
CLM-126.strength: expert consensus recommendation (systematic review + Delphi, 89 IOIBD members; 13 of 15 recommendations endorsed)
CLM-126.owner: Deferred by owner: STRIDE-II superseded by STRIDE-III (PMID 42896564); see candidate CLM-703.

authored_sources.title: Updated treatment targets in inflammatory bowel disease (STRIDE-III): an initiative of the International Organization for the Study of IBD
authored_sources.note: Added at the owner's request (supersedes STRIDE-II). Published before the 2026-11-10 discovery start, so daily discovery never saw it.

reissued_live.claimText: A European consensus statement (ECCO, 2025) gives low-level, expert-opinion advice (evidence level 5; 100% agreement among panel members) for people with inflammatory bowel disease in general, not just ulcerative colitis: unless an IBD clinician recommends a specific diet, follow the healthy-eating guidelines for the general population. This is general, low-evidence IBD-wide advice, not a UC-specific treatment.
reissued_live.supportingExcerpt: Statement 1: In the absence of a specific dietary intervention that is recommended by an IBD healthcare professional, healthy eating guidelines should be followed by people with IBD, as recommended for the general population. (EL5) (Consensus: 100%)
reissued_live.limitations: Low-evidence (EL5) expert consensus for IBD in general; not specific to ulcerative colitis. Re-issue of live claim CLM-081 with clearer labelling (owner decision 2026-11-17); the original is preserved in prototype-v1.

reissued_live.claimText: A patient-information page from Crohn's & Colitis UK says there is not enough high-quality evidence to know for certain whether drinking alcohol could increase your risk of a flare-up. This is a statement of uncertainty: it does not mean alcohol is safe, and it does not mean it is harmful for you. Talk to your clinician about alcohol.
reissued_live.supportingExcerpt: Alcohol There is not enough high-quality evidence to know for certain if drinking alcohol could increase your risk of a flare-up.
reissued_live.limitations: Statement of uncertainty from patient information (not a study); applies to IBD in general. Re-issue of live claim CLM-095 with an explicit 'not proven safe' wording (owner decision 2026-11-17); the original is preserved in prototype-v1.
